segments.title: Iron Duke as Jellicoe's flagship
segments.body: Iron Duke represents the mature end of Britain's 13.5-inch battleship development. Eighteen water-tube boilers produced 29,000 shaft horsepower and 21.4 knots. A 12-inch belt and a range of 7,718 nautical miles at 10 knots completed a balanced design that few contemporary German ships could comfortably face. The class followed three British classes armed with 12-inch guns and three with 13.5-inch guns, refining an established pattern rather than testing an uncertain concept. Admiral John Jellicoe kept Iron Duke as his flagship after the Queen Elizabeth class entered service because it still suited his needs.

evidence.note: The video gives Iron Duke's guns, boilers, speed, belt, range, and Jellicoe flagship discussion.

segments.summary: The Iron Duke class combined 13.5-inch guns, a 12-inch belt, and 21-knot performance in the balanced flagship Admiral Jellicoe chose to retain.

segments.title: Nevada and the American standard battleship
segments.body: Nevada marked the arrival of the American standard battleship. Its ten 14-inch guns matched Iron Duke's gun count at a larger calibre, and the United States Navy's move to triple turrets increased the technological pressure on British designers. Nevada's turbines and Oklahoma's triple-expansion engines also provided a direct machinery comparison within the same class. Both ships had nominal speeds of 20.5 knots and ranges of 8,000 nautical miles at 10 knots, although those figures did not promise identical sustained performance. A thick armour belt helped make the class one of the stronger battleship designs of the period.

evidence.note: The video discusses Nevada's 14-inch guns, triple turret, Nevada and Oklahoma machinery, range, and armour belt.

segments.summary: Nevada's 14-inch battery and triple turrets marked the arrival of the American standard battleship, while its machinery comparison with Oklahoma exposed propulsion trade-offs.

segments.title: Derfflinger's uncertain return on investment
segments.body: Derfflinger finally moved German battlecruisers from 11-inch weapons to eight 12-inch guns. Its superfiring arrangement improved forward fire, yet other navies had already adopted heavier batteries. Lutzow and Hindenburg received more 15-centimetre secondary guns and larger torpedo tubes, while the armour belt remained close to that of earlier German battlecruisers. The design only appears equivalent to newer British ships if German 12-inch performance is treated as matching British 13.5-inch guns, an equivalence the episode rejects. This makes the class a procurement problem: an expensive capital ship needed to add enough combat capability to justify its cost.

evidence.note: The video evaluates Derfflinger's 12-inch armament, firing arrangement, secondary battery, torpedo tubes, armour, cost, and capability.

segments.summary: The Derfflinger class finally brought 12-inch guns to German battlecruisers, although its armament and fittings offered an uncertain return against stronger foreign designs.

segments.title: Borodino's fast battleship role
segments.body: Borodino sits on the fast-battleship spectrum, a choice suited to Russia's constrained access from the Black Sea and Baltic. A Russian force might have to fight through an opponent before reaching wider operating waters, making speed and heavy firepower useful together. Four triple turrets on one level produced a twelve-gun 14-inch broadside while retaining a claimed speed of 26.5 knots. That battery greatly outweighed Derfflinger's eight 12-inch guns, and Russian gunnery had become effective by the First World War. The comparison shows how strategic geography and an expected fighting role could produce a very different capital-ship design.

evidence.note: The video links Borodino to Russian operating geography and discusses its triple turrets, twelve 14-inch guns, speed, armour, and comparison with Derfflinger.

segments.summary: Russia's Borodino class paired twelve 14-inch guns with fast-battleship speed for the demanding routes from the Black and Baltic seas.

segments.title: Queen Elizabeth raises the calibre stakes
segments.body: Britain's move from 13.5-inch to 15-inch guns appears here as a response to other navies adopting 14-inch weapons, especially the United States. The increase was larger than Britain needed merely to overmatch contemporary German guns. The familiar 1.5-inch increments were a practical logistical pattern rather than an inflexible rule. When foreign designers later considered 16-inch weapons, British planning could look past a hypothetical 16.5-inch step toward 18-inch battleship guns. A 16-inch option for a battlecruiser would preserve the speed that type required, keeping calibre tied to role and machinery.

evidence.note: The video links the 15-inch-gun step to foreign 14-inch batteries, British logistical increments, and later 16-inch and 18-inch planning.

segments.summary: Britain's jump from 13.5-inch to 15-inch guns answered the wider spread of 14-inch batteries and anticipated another round of capital-ship gun escalation.

segments.title: Queen Elizabeth trades a fifth turret for speed
segments.body: The Queen Elizabeth hull preserves evidence of a live trade-off between a fifth 15-inch turret and more propulsion power. Britain chose eight heavy guns and used the available volume for twenty-four water-tube boilers driving four shafts at 75,000 shaft horsepower. The resulting 24-knot speed narrowed the margin on which German battlecruisers relied to disengage. A 13-inch waterline belt preserved battleship protection rather than gaining speed through battlecruiser vulnerability. The design combined heavier firepower, protection, and greater speed without reaching the limit of British construction capacity.

evidence.note: The video identifies the fifth-turret space, 24 boilers, four shafts, 75,000 shaft horsepower, 13-inch belt, and 24-knot speed.

segments.summary: Queen Elizabeth's unused fifth-turret space reveals the choice to put machinery and 24-knot speed ahead of two more 15-inch guns.

segments.title: Andrea Doria and a navy built for its waters
segments.body: The Andrea Doria class was a coherent response to the opponents and waters Italy expected to face. Thirteen 12-inch guns provided ample weight of fire for that mission even as other navies moved to larger calibres. A speed of about 21 knots and useful protection completed a conventional, purposeful Mediterranean battleship. Italy did not need to copy every North Sea escalation when its likely enemies and operating area posed a different design problem. That clear fit between mission and design contrasts with the episode's uncertainty about what strategic task German capital ships were built to accomplish.

evidence.note: The video describes Andrea Doria's armament, speed, protection, intended fighting areas, and contrast with German design purpose.

segments.summary: Italy's Andrea Doria class kept 12-inch guns and 21-knot speed because its design matched Mediterranean priorities rather than a direct North Sea contest.

segments.title: The 1912 balance of dreadnought fleets
segments.body: Ships in service and under construction show the Royal Navy pulling away from its rivals in 1912. Britain had roughly eighteen dreadnoughts and battlecruisers in service and twelve more under construction, while Germany's eight operational ships and ten building already looked outmatched. The United States also fielded eight and had four under construction, making it a major part of the global balance. French, Italian, Austro-Hungarian, Brazilian, Japanese, Australian, Ottoman, Chilean, and Spanish programmes broaden the picture beyond the North Sea. Hull totals posed a separate strategic problem from the latest gun, armour, or propulsion specification.

evidence.note: The video surveys dreadnought and battlecruiser numbers in service and construction across the major naval powers.

segments.summary: A 1912 fleet count shows the Royal Navy pulling ahead while the United States, France, Italy, Japan, and several smaller powers continued to add dreadnoughts.

segments.title: A two-level global naval race
segments.body: The prewar dreadnought race had two interacting levels. Germany's risk-fleet strategy tried to make war too costly for Britain by threatening enough of the Royal Navy's numerical strength. A technological competition unfolded at the same time, with Italian research and published ideas contributing differently from American ships entering construction. Britain needed to protect its numerical lead and its qualitative advantage. The Royal Navy therefore sought a margin in hulls over Germany while keeping ahead of other capital-ship builders in technology.

evidence.note: The video distinguishes Germany's hull-number and risk-fleet challenge from the technological competition involving Italian research and American construction.

segments.summary: The 1912 naval race combined Germany's risk-fleet challenge in hull numbers with technological pressure from American construction and Italian research.

segments.title: German gun calibre follows rather than drives
segments.body: The order in which navies adopted larger guns complicates the usual account of the naval race. A numerically inferior challenger might use heavier weapons to compensate for having fewer hulls, so Germany should have led calibre growth if it drove that part of the competition. German capital ships instead followed British increases. Britain had little need to enlarge its guns merely to outbuild the German fleet in numbers. American willingness to build fewer ships with 14-inch batteries supplied the more immediate technological pressure, forcing Britain to protect its qualitative lead as well as its numerical one.

evidence.note: The video argues that larger guns could offset fewer hulls, observes that German calibres followed British increases, and identifies American construction as the stronger pressure.

segments.summary: Germany's delayed adoption of larger guns undercuts the idea that its fleet drove British calibre growth and missed a way to offset numerical inferiority.

segments.title: Reading past the two-sided naval-race story
segments.body: Many short histories make the prewar naval race look like a self-contained contest between Britain and Germany. Reading Massie, Lambert, and other historians reveals technological exchange and competition among several navies. American 14-inch battleships mattered because Britain would not accept foreign ships carrying a visibly larger main battery. Queen Elizabeth therefore answered American technological pressure as well as German hull numbers. Germany produced no immediate equivalent and instead chased a standard Britain had raised again.

evidence.note: The video contrasts simplified two-sided histories with deeper reading in Massie, Lambert, and others, then ties Queen Elizabeth to the American technological challenge.

segments.summary: A wider reading of Massie, Lambert, and other historians reveals global technological interplay hidden by a purely Anglo-German narrative.
